The Zerodha Life Cycle Fund series follows a simple, rule-based investing philosophy. It currently comprises two maturity variants – Zerodha Life Cycle Fund 2036, with a 10-year maturity horizon, and Zerodha Life Cycle Fund 2041, with a 15-year maturity horizon. Over time, additional schemes with varying maturity years will be introduced to cater to investors across different life stages and financial goals.  
Zerodha Life Cycle Fund 2036 will be benchmarked against a composite index comprising 50% Nifty 200 TRI, 5% domestic prices of physical gold, 5% domestic prices of physical silver, and 40% CRISIL 10-Year Gilt Index. Zerodha Life Cycle Fund 2041 will be benchmarked against 65% Nifty 200 TRI, 5% domestic prices of physical gold, 5% domestic prices of physical silver, and 25% CRISIL 10-Year Gilt Index. Both schemes will be managed by Kedarnath Mirajkar.  
ET logo
Live Events
On the equity side, the funds aim to track the Nifty LargeMidcap 250 Index. For debt exposure, they invest in Indian government securities (G-secs) across different durations, while also maintaining exposure to commodities and arbitrage strategies.  
Globally, target-date funds manage assets exceeding $4 trillion and serve as the default retirement investment vehicle for millions of investors. Zerodha said it aims to bring this concept to India through a simple, transparent and goal-based structure.  
“The mutual fund industry has historically been organised around products. We believe the next phase of investing will be organised around goals. Target-date funds, as a category, have transformed long-term investing globally, and we're excited to introduce something similar to Indian investors for the first time. We believe it has the potential to become the default long-term investment option for a generation of Indian investors,” said Vishal Jain, CEO of Zerodha Fund House.  
The funds will be classified as equity for taxation purposes throughout their lifecycle, allowing investors to benefit from long-term capital gains tax treatment. There is no lock-in period, and investors may exit at any time, subject to applicable exit loads.  
The minimum investment amount is Rs 100. At maturity, investors may either redeem their holdings or remain invested if the fund is merged with the nearest maturity Life Cycle fund, in accordance with regulations.  
Also Read |Mutual funds cut PSU bank exposure to 8-month low in May. Warning sign or buying opportunity?   
“Indian mutual fund investors now have a multi-asset fund built around a finish line. You choose your target year, and the fund aims to build wealth until that date. Whether it is your child’s education, buying a home or saving for retirement, Life Cycle funds keep your asset allocation aligned with your target year,” said Vaibhav Jalan, CBO of Zerodha Fund House.  
Each Life Cycle fund is structured around a specific maturity year, known as the target year, and invests across a diversified mix of equity, debt and commodities such as gold and silver.  
The portfolio follows a pre-defined asset allocation path that gradually shifts from a growth-oriented (higher-risk) allocation in the early years to a more conservative (lower-risk) allocation as the target year approaches. As a result, an investor’s portfolio evolves over time automatically, without requiring any action from the investor.

author-image
Sumit Vishwakarma
 Follow Us
New Update
Indian brokerage Zerodha has launched US stock investing through its Kite platform, allowing eligible investors to buy shares in American companies and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) using their existing accounts.
Advertisment
banner/indianstartupnews/media/media_files/2026/06/17/desktop-728-x-90-1-2026-06-17-17-20-35.png)
The service provides access to up to 2,000 US-listed companies and around 1,000 ETFs, with fractional investments starting at $1.
Resident Indian individuals can activate the international investing segment without opening a separate demat account. The facility is not available to non-resident Indians (NRIs), joint account holders or non-individual entities.
The offering is routed through BSE-owned India INX Global Access at the International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) in Gujarat's GIFT City.
Zerodha's official investing guide identifies ViewTrade as its US brokerage partner. Securities purchased through the platform are held through the overseas broker rather than in an Indian demat account.
What are the charges for US stock investing?
Zerodha charges brokerage of 0.1% of the transaction value, subject to a minimum of $0.01 and a maximum of $10 per executed order. The fee applies to both purchases and sales, with an additional 18% goods and services tax (GST) on brokerage.
The brokerage cap means a $20,000 transaction would attract a $10 fee instead of $20 under an uncapped 0.1% rate, excluding taxes and any other applicable charges.
There is, however, a discrepancy in Zerodha's published information on regulatory fees. Its detailed investing guide lists an IFSC Authority (IFSCA) turnover fee of 0.005% of the trade value and applicable US regulatory fees on sales, while the company's main US-investing page states that these charges are included in brokerage.
The detailed guide also said the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority's (FINRA) Trading Activity Fee is suspended from 1 October to 31 December 2026.
Currency conversion is another consideration. Zerodha's current investing guide states that it has negotiated a bank markup of 0.5% above the Reserve Bank of India's reference exchange rate. Banks may also levy remittance charges and applicable taxes.
For comparison, rival brokerage Groww lists a 0.1% brokerage fee for US stock transactions, subject to a minimum of $1 per executed order. Its published pricing does not specify a maximum brokerage cap.
How can investors buy US stocks?
Investors can transfer money from their linked Indian bank accounts into a dollar-denominated Global wallet through netbanking.
The service currently supports transfers through HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Axis Bank, Kotak Mahindra Bank and IDFC FIRST Bank. UPI, debit cards and credit cards cannot be used.
Although fractional investments begin at $1, Zerodha requires a minimum initial fund transfer of $50, followed by at least $100 for subsequent transfers.
The platform supports delivery-based investing in eligible stocks and ETFs, including purchases of fractional shares. Market and limit orders are available, but intraday trading, margin trading and derivatives are not supported.
Investors also cannot apply for US initial public offerings (IPOs) through the platform. Newly listed shares become available for purchase only if they meet Zerodha's eligibility requirements.
The ETF offering is restricted to eligible funds with assets under management exceeding $250 million. Bitcoin ETFs and leveraged ETFs are excluded.
Overseas investments are subject to the Reserve Bank of India's Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), under which resident individuals can remit up to $250,000 per financial year across permitted purposes.
Investors must also comply with applicable tax collected at source (TCS) requirements and foreign asset disclosure rules.
Competition intensifies in overseas investing
Zerodha's entry comes as rival Indian stockbrokers, including Groww and Upstox, expand beyond domestic equities to offer retail investors direct access to international markets.
The new services compete with established overseas investment providers such as INDmoney and HDFC Securities, which already offer Indian investors access to American equities.
The expansion comes amid growing interest in geographical diversification and direct exposure to global technology companies, particularly those operating in AI, cloud computing and semiconductors.
US-listed companies such as Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon offer exposure to major global businesses that investors may not be able to replicate through domestic equities alone.
Interest in American technology listings has also been heightened by high-profile market debuts, including SpaceX's Nasdaq listing in June 2026.
However, direct investment in US equities carries risks beyond movements in share prices. Currency fluctuations, foreign exchange costs, taxation and regulatory obligations can all affect returns, making the overall cost of investing an important consideration when choosing a platform.
